operations.evidence: The Met Office warning operation runs 24 hours a day and 365 days a year.
Continuous operation does not mean a warning is active for every hazard or location.
Warnings can be provided up to seven days ahead.
The maximum horizon does not imply equal certainty across all seven days.
Warnings cover rain, thunderstorms, wind, snow, lightning, ice, extreme heat and fog.
The hazard list is not an exhaustive inventory of every local public-safety threat.
Warnings contain a headline, what to expect, what to do and further details.
Structured sections support interpretation but do not convert forecasts into observed impacts.
National Severe Weather Warning Service warnings use yellow, amber and red colours.
Colour must not be treated as a standalone numeric risk score.
Warning colour is determined from a combination of potential impact and likelihood.
Neither colour nor likelihood alone identifies exact impact at a particular parcel.
The warning's further details show an impact matrix with the selected impact-likelihood combination.
The matrix is a forecast communication tool and not an event verification record.
Yellow warnings can represent likely low-level impacts or lower-certainty scenarios with more severe potential impacts.
Yellow cannot be translated to one fixed severity without reading the warning content and matrix.
Amber indicates increased likelihood of severe-weather impacts including possible travel disruption, closures, power cuts and risk to life or property.
The listed impacts are possibilities across the warning area and not confirmed outcomes at every location.
Warning impact levels are very low, low, medium and high.
Impact level is categorical and should not be used as a parcel loss estimate.
Not every location in a warning area will necessarily experience the same impact level.
Area coverage must not be spatially joined as uniform parcel exposure.
Previous weather conditions can change impacts, such as saturated ground increasing flooding from modest rainfall.
A hazard threshold must not be interpreted without antecedent-condition context.
When severe impacts are expected, impacts at lower levels are also likely.
Nested impacts do not justify double-counting the same event across severity categories.
Users are instructed to read the warning details and matrix rather than rely on colour alone.
Any automated candidate must retain headline, impact, likelihood and geographic context.
Weather-health alerts are issued by UKHSA in partnership with the Met Office.
A joint alert is a population-health warning and not a clinical record for an individual.
The system monitors hot and cold episodes that may affect health and issues an appropriate alert after assessment.
A forecast health impact does not prove morbidity or mortality at a named location.
The system includes Heat-Health Alerts and Cold-Health Alerts.
The two components must not be combined without preserving season and hazard type.
The Heat-Health Alert core season operates from 1 June to 30 September.
Core-season dates do not prevent exceptional alerts outside the season.
The April 2026 user guide states that the Cold-Health Alert season operates from 1 November to 30 March.
Season-end wording should be versioned because other landing-page text may use a different end-date convention.
An out-of-season heat or cold alert may be issued when health impacts are expected.
Absence of a core-season alert does not prove absence of weather-related health risk.
UKHSA and the Met Office conduct a joint dynamic risk assessment when forecast hot or cold episodes meet predefined considerations.
The assessment is dynamic and must not be represented as a static parcel score.
Alert decisions use predefined evidence-based considerations alongside weather forecasts.
The publication does not expose a parcel-level deterministic threshold for every alert decision.
Registered users can select the government region for which they receive alerts.
Government-region targeting is much coarser than parcel geography.
Alert levels trigger communication of risk to NHS England, government and the public-health system.
Communication activation does not establish realised health outcomes.
After an alert is issued or updated, advice is sent to the public and health and social-care professionals, especially those supporting at-risk groups.
Advice distribution is a preparedness action rather than evidence of individual exposure.
UKHSA Weather-Health Alerts are separate from the Met Office National Severe Weather Warning Service and focus specifically on health impacts.
The two systems must not be deduplicated solely because they reference the same weather episode.
The Adverse Weather and Health Plan aims to protect individuals and communities from health effects of adverse weather and build resilience.
The plan is a preparedness framework and not evidence that a local organisation has implemented every action.
The plan seeks to prevent additional mortality and morbidity, reduce years of life lost and reduce healthcare use caused by adverse weather.
Programme aims are not measured outcome values for a specific event or locality.
The plan identifies nine action areas including service delivery, capacity, organisational arrangements, communication, risk management, early warning, research, quality assurance and accountability.
The action-area list is a planning framework and not a compliance score for an organisation.
